title: Styling in Next.js (CSS Modules, Global CSS, Tailwind, Fonts)
summary: Next.js supports several ways to style a page, including CSS Modules and global CSS.

subtopics.title: Global CSS
subtopics.explanation: Global CSS can affect many elements across the application. It is useful for resets, base typography, and shared styles. It is like a building-wide rule about lighting. Keep global selectors modest because a broad change can alter unrelated pages. In Next.js, follow the project’s supported place for importing global styles. For example, use global CSS for a small set of app-wide defaults, not page-specific selectors.

subtopics.title: CSS Modules
subtopics.explanation: A CSS Module scopes its class names to a file when imported by a component. This lowers the chance that two components accidentally use the same style name. It is like a label that only applies inside one folder. Modules are useful for component-specific styles that should not leak elsewhere. For example, keep a CSS Module next to a component when its styles should stay local.

subtopics.title: Use module classes
subtopics.explanation: Import a CSS Module and use its exported class names on elements. The build system maps them to generated names while preserving the local reference in code. It is like using a local nickname that is translated to a unique label. Keep the module close to its component so changes are easy to locate. For example, share spacing tokens through CSS variables so one design adjustment updates related parts.

subtopics.title: Shared values
subtopics.explanation: CSS variables can store colors, spacing, and other values used across components. A shared token lets a theme change one value instead of many separate rules. It is like a palette card used by the whole design team. Name variables by purpose and ensure contrast remains readable when themes change. For example, use responsive rules when a layout no longer fits, not only at arbitrary device labels.

subtopics.title: Responsive rules
subtopics.explanation: Responsive rules adapt the page to different screen sizes and user settings. Use flexible layouts and add breakpoints when the content needs a real change. It is like rearranging furniture in a smaller room. Check navigation, forms, and text at narrow widths and high zoom. For example, test font and color behavior after switching the application theme.

foundations.overview: Next.js supports several ways to style a page. Global CSS is shared across the app, while CSS Modules keep class names local to a file. You can also use design tokens and utility frameworks. Think of global styles as building-wide rules and module styles as labels kept with one component. Pick a consistent approach, keep shared values deliberate, and test responsive layouts.
foundations.whyItMatters: A consistent styling approach helps a Next.js app grow without accidental style collisions. Keep global decisions small and component styles close to the behavior they support.
foundations.browserPerspective: The browser receives static, extracted CSS in <link>/<style> tags that it can apply immediately as HTML paints — no waiting for JS. With runtime CSS-in-JS, styles may be generated by JavaScript, risking a flash of unstyled content unless the framework injects critical CSS during SSR.
foundations.realWorldUsage: A typical app imports globals.css (resets + CSS variables) in the root layout, uses Tailwind for most components, and applies a next/font className on <body>. Teams preferring plain CSS use CSS Modules per component instead of Tailwind.
foundations.businessImpact: Consistent, fast-loading styles improve perceived quality and Core Web Vitals (which influence SEO and conversion). A maintainable styling system also speeds feature delivery and reduces visual regressions.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Choosing build-time, scoped styling reduces collisions and runtime cost, making the codebase easier to refactor. Misusing global CSS or runtime CSS-in-JS in Server Components leads to leaks, FOUC, and 'use client' creep.
foundations.performanceImpact: Tailwind and CSS Modules extract static CSS that's tree-shaken and CDN-cacheable, adding no JS. Runtime CSS-in-JS ships extra JavaScript and computes styles on the client, increasing bundle size and hydration work. next/font removes render-blocking font requests and prevents layout shift.
commonUseCases: Global CSS for resets and design tokens (CSS variables)
CSS Modules for component-scoped styles without a utility framework
Tailwind for fast, consistent utility-driven styling with small CSS output
next/font to self-host fonts and eliminate font-related layout shift

commonMisconceptions.myth: styled-components and Emotion work everywhere in the App Router.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Runtime CSS-in-JS needs client execution and a StyleRegistry; it does not work in Server Components by default and adds runtime cost.

commonMisconceptions.myth: CSS Modules add a runtime performance cost like CSS-in-JS.
commonMisconceptions.reality: CSS Modules are extracted to static CSS at build time — they only change class names and ship no JavaScript.

commonMisconceptions.myth: You can import global CSS anywhere in the App Router.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Global stylesheets should be imported in the root layout (or a Server Component); arbitrary global imports are restricted to keep ordering predictable.

commonMisconceptions.myth: CSS Modules eliminate the need to think about global styles.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Resets, inherited properties, and global rules can still affect module elements.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Tailwind or another utility system removes CSS design decisions.
commonMisconceptions.reality: A utility framework still needs deliberate responsive, accessible, and maintainable choices.

visualExplorer.title: Choosing a styling approach
visualExplorer.caption: Walk through each styling option in Next.js and where it fits.

config.intro: Step through the main styling choices and what each is best for.

steps.name: Global CSS
steps.detail: Imported once in the root layout. Unscoped — great for resets and CSS-variable design tokens, risky for component styles because selectors leak.

steps.name: CSS Modules
steps.detail: *.module.css files are scoped by hashing class names. Plain CSS, no collisions, build-time extracted, works in Server and Client Components.

steps.name: Tailwind
steps.detail: Utility classes composed in JSX. Build-time static CSS, tree-shaken to only used classes, zero runtime JS — ideal with Server Components.

steps.name: CSS-in-JS
steps.detail: styled-components/Emotion compute styles in JS at runtime. Needs 'use client' + a StyleRegistry for SSR; adds bundle and hydration cost.

steps.name: next/font
steps.detail: Self-hosts fonts at build time, returns a className/CSS variable, removes render-blocking requests and prevents layout shift (CLS).

codeLab.title: Pick the right styling tool per need
codeLab.instructions: For each styling need, fill in the best approach (Global CSS, CSS Modules, Tailwind, or next/font) and one reason. Edit the component and Run.
codeLab.expectedOutput: Your reasoned choice for each styling need.
hints: Ask: is it global, component-local, a utility, or a font concern?
Global tokens → globals.css; scoped CSS → Modules; utilities → Tailwind; fonts → next/font.

keyTakeaways: Global CSS can affect many elements across the application.
A CSS Module scopes its class names to a file when imported by a component.
Import a CSS Module and use its exported class names on elements.
CSS variables can store colors, spacing, and other values used across components.
Responsive rules adapt the page to different screen sizes and user settings.
